twist.stem: A dig finds one district with streets crossing at right angles and another with winding lanes. What is the fairest claim?
twist.hint: Judge each part by its own street pattern.

options.text: The whole city was planned, since part of it was.
options.feedback: A grid shows a plan only where it is found. The winding district may have grown bit by bit.

options.text: Only the grid district shows a plan.
options.feedback: Yes. Right-angle streets point to a plan, so each district is judged by its own layout.

options.text: Neither was planned; grids can form by chance.
options.feedback: A neat grid does not grow by chance. Right-angle streets point to a plan.

transfer.stem: A drone survey over farmland in Haryana shows buried walls meeting at neat right angles in long straight rows. What is the fairest first claim?
transfer.hint: A grid does not grow by chance.

options.text: People planned the layout before building.
options.feedback: Right. Walls in straight rows at right angles point to a plan, just as Mohenjo-daro's grid does.

options.text: Walls like that pile up by chance as houses are added.
options.feedback: Houses added bit by bit give winding lanes and odd corners. A neat grid points to a plan.

options.text: It must have been a royal palace.
options.feedback: A grid shows a plan, not what the buildings were for. Who used them needs other evidence.

twist.stem: A student draws Mohenjo-daro with open mud ditches along the main roads only. How many mistakes are in the drawing?
twist.hint: Check where they ran and how they were built.

options.text: One: the drains were brick, but just on main roads.
options.feedback: Not only main roads: every street and lane had a drain. So the drawing has two mistakes.

options.text: None; that fits what was dug up.
options.feedback: The dig found drains on every street and lane, and most were covered with brick, not open mud.

options.text: Two: lanes had drains, mostly covered.
options.feedback: Yes. Every street and lane had a drain, and most were covered with baked bricks, not open ditches.

transfer.stem: Lakshmi is building a house in a Kerala town and wants used kitchen water to leave without wetting the lane. Which Mohenjo-daro plan does she copy?
transfer.hint: Follow the water out of the home.

options.text: Letting the water run down the open lane.
options.feedback: In Mohenjo-daro, water went from homes into covered drains, not down the open lane.

options.text: A pipe from the house into a covered street drain.
options.feedback: Right. Mohenjo-daro homes sent used water through pipes and chutes into covered drains along every street.

options.text: A pit in her yard, since old cities had no drains.
options.feedback: Mohenjo-daro had drains on every street and lane, fed by pipes from homes.

twist.stem: A video claims we now know everything about Mohenjo-daro. What is the best reply?
twist.hint: How much has been dug, and can we read the signs?

options.text: True; the whole city has been dug up.
options.feedback: Only about a third of the city has been dug, so much of it is still unknown.

options.text: True, since the seals have now been read.
options.feedback: No one can read the Indus script yet, so the seals do not tell us their meaning.

options.text: A third is dug, and the script is unread.
options.feedback: Yes. Most of the city is still buried, and the signs cannot be read, so much is still unknown.

transfer.stem: Rohit finds his great-grandmother's diary in a script no one at home can read, along with old photos and a brass lamp. What can the family learn for now?
transfer.hint: Keep what you can see apart from what you guess.

options.text: Everything, by guessing the words from the photos.
options.feedback: Guessing words from photos is not reading. Like the Indus seals, the diary's text stays unknown until it can be read.

options.text: What the photos and objects themselves show.
options.feedback: Right. As with the unread Indus script, they can learn from what survives, but not from words they cannot read.

options.text: Very little until the diary is read.
options.feedback: Objects and photos still tell a story, just as streets, drains and baths tell us about Mohenjo-daro.

twist.stem: A museum label claims Ashoka's edicts survive only on his palace walls. What is wrong with it?
twist.hint: Think of where passers-by could see them.

options.text: Rocks and pillars across the empire held his words.
options.feedback: Yes. Ashoka had his words carved on natural rocks and polished pillars near towns and routes, not only at court.

options.text: They were painted on palm leaves and cloth, not walls.
options.feedback: Ashoka's edicts were carved in stone, on rocks and pillars, which is why some still stand.

options.text: The label is right; the edicts stayed at court.
options.feedback: The edicts were carved on rocks and pillars near towns and routes, so passers-by could see them.

transfer.stem: A district health team in Madhya Pradesh wants a vaccine notice seen by most villagers for years. Using Ashoka's idea, where would it go?
transfer.hint: Think about who walks past each spot, and what lasts.

options.text: One copy in the collector's office.
options.feedback: An office is seen by few people. Ashoka put his words near towns and routes, where many passed.

options.text: A paper notice inside the clinic, changed each month.
options.feedback: Paper inside a room fades and reaches few. Ashoka chose lasting stone in places many people passed.

options.text: Painted stone boards at bus stands and markets.
options.feedback: Right. Like Ashoka's carved stones near busy routes, it is placed where crowds pass and made to last.

twist.stem: An edict from the northwest, outside Afghanistan, is not written in Brahmi. Which script is it most likely in?
twist.hint: Afghanistan used Greek and Aramaic. What about the rest of the northwest?

options.text: Greek, as in Afghanistan.
options.feedback: Greek was used in Afghanistan. Other edicts in the northwest used Kharosthi.

options.text: Kharosthi.
options.feedback: Yes. Some edicts in the northwest used Kharosthi, while those in Afghanistan used Greek and Aramaic.

options.text: Aramaic, as everywhere outside Bihar.
options.feedback: Aramaic was used in Afghanistan. Most of the empire used Brahmi, and parts of the northwest used Kharosthi.

transfer.stem: An app maker in Bengaluru wants one message read in many Indian states. Following Ashoka's way, what would she do?
transfer.hint: Did one way of writing fit the whole empire?

options.text: Use the capital's script in each state.
options.feedback: Ashoka did not use one capital script. His edicts changed script from region to region.

options.text: Use one script, as Ashoka did.
options.feedback: Ashoka did not use one script. Brahmi, Kharosthi, Greek and Aramaic were used in different regions.

options.text: Write it in each region's own script.
options.feedback: Right. Ashoka's edicts changed script by region, from Brahmi to Kharosthi, Greek and Aramaic.

twist.stem: Which of these lines would fit in an edict about Ashoka's dhamma?
twist.hint: Think of how people treat each other.

options.text: Be kind to servants and respect elders.
options.feedback: Yes. Dhamma asked people to be kind to servants, respect elders and respect other faiths.

options.text: Pray at the king's temple for peace.
options.feedback: Dhamma asked people to respect faiths not their own, not to pray at one royal temple.

options.text: Give the king a share of your harvest each year.
options.feedback: Dhamma was about respect and kindness in daily life, not about gifts to the king.

transfer.stem: A hostel warden in Pune writes house rules in the spirit of Ashoka's dhamma. Which rule fits best?
transfer.hint: Dhamma was about how people treat each other.

options.text: Respect each other's faiths and festivals.
options.feedback: Right. Dhamma asked people to respect other faiths, as well as elders and those who serve them.

options.text: Share one prayer each morning for all of you.
options.feedback: A shared prayer can feel kind, but dhamma asked for respect for faiths not your own, not one prayer for all.

options.text: Keep quiet about faith to avoid clashes.
options.feedback: Dhamma did not ask people to hide their faith. It asked them to respect faiths not their own.

twist.stem: A ship lands cloth at a west coast port. What is the next leg of its trip toward Gandhara?
twist.hint: Follow the order in the example.

options.text: Over the high mountain passes.
options.feedback: The passes come after Gandhara, on the way to China. From the coast, goods first went up the Indus.

options.text: Across the deserts of Central Asia.
options.feedback: Central Asia lies beyond the passes. From the coast, goods first went up the Indus to Gandhara.

options.text: Up the Indus River.
options.feedback: Yes. From the west coast, goods went up the Indus to Gandhara, and only then over the passes.

transfer.stem: A trader in Kochi sends spices to a hill town in Himachal by ship, then by train, then by mountain road. Which Silk Road idea does this match?
transfer.hint: Was the Silk Road one road?

options.text: Trade needs one single road from end to end.
options.feedback: The Silk Road was not one road. Goods moved by sea, river and mountain pass in turn.

options.text: Linked sea, land and mountain routes.
options.feedback: Right. The Silk Road linked sea, river and mountain routes, and this trip links three kinds of route too.

options.text: Goods moved by land, not by sea.
options.feedback: Ships crossed the sea to India's west coast, so the routes mixed sea and land.

twist.stem: A valley far from the mountain passes saw little trade and has few Buddhist carvings. What best explains this?
twist.hint: Ask what paid for the art.

options.text: Less trade meant less wealth to pay for art.
options.feedback: Yes. In Gandhara, trade wealth paid for Buddhist art, so a valley with little trade had less to spend.

options.text: Its people did not care for art.
options.feedback: The pattern points to money, not taste. Gandhara's art was paid for by trade through the passes.

options.text: Faith alone made art, so trade did not matter.
options.feedback: Faith mattered, but the carving was paid for. In Gandhara, trade wealth paid for the art.

transfer.stem: In a mill town in Tamil Nadu, the mills close and the town's drama troupes lose their sponsors. Which Gandhara pattern does this match?
transfer.hint: What paid for Gandhara's art?

options.text: Art lasts on faith alone, whatever the money.
options.feedback: In Gandhara, art grew because trade made the region rich. When money falls, art loses its support.

options.text: Art depends on rulers, not on trade.
options.feedback: Gandhara's art was paid for by the wealth trade brought, not by rulers alone.

options.text: Less trade wealth, less money for art.
options.feedback: Right. Trade wealth paid for Gandhara's art, so when the money from trade drops, art loses its support.

twist.stem: Why did monks from Gandhara move into Central Asia?
twist.hint: Think of who invaded.

options.text: Traders seem to have paid them to leave.
options.feedback: Traders were not the reason. Hun invasions seem to have driven the monks out.

options.text: Their art style seems to have been banned at home.
options.feedback: Their style was not banned. Hun invasions seem to have forced the monks to move.

options.text: Hun invasions seem to have driven them out.
options.feedback: Yes. Hun invasions appear to have forced the monks out, and their art took root in Central Asia.

transfer.stem: Dosa stalls are now common in Delhi, far from where dosa began. How did that most likely happen?
transfer.hint: Ideas need someone to take them.

options.text: The recipe spread on its own, with no one carrying it.
options.feedback: Ideas do not travel alone. Like Gandhara's art, a recipe moves when people who know it move.

options.text: People who knew how to make it moved there.
options.feedback: Right. Ideas move with people, just as Gandhara's monks carried their art style to Central Asia.

options.text: Delhi cooks made it up again by chance.
options.feedback: The simpler story is people moving with the skill, as Gandhara's monks took their style with them.

twist.stem: In the number 4,006, what do the two zeros tell you?
twist.hint: Read each spot from the left.

options.text: They can be dropped without changing it.
options.feedback: Dropping them would turn 4,006 into 46. Each zero keeps an empty spot.

options.text: There are no hundreds and no tens.
options.feedback: Yes. Each zero marks an empty spot, so 4,006 has 4 thousands, no hundreds, no tens and 6 ones.

options.text: The number is close to zero.
options.feedback: The zeros mark empty spots, not a small number. 4,006 still has 4 thousands.

transfer.stem: A cricket scoreboard in Indore shows 104 with one tile per place. The tens tile falls off, and the other tiles slide together. What might fans read?
transfer.hint: What happens when an empty place is not marked?

options.text: 104, since the tiles keep their places.
options.feedback: The tiles slid together, so the empty tens spot vanished. Without a zero, 104 reads as 14.

options.text: 140, since the zero moves to the end.
options.feedback: Nothing moves to the end. Without the zero, the 1 and 4 sit side by side and read 14.

options.text: 14 runs.
options.feedback: Right. The zero was holding the empty tens place. Without it, the 1 slides down and 104 reads as 14.

twist.stem: Zero as a sign for an empty place came first. What did Brahmagupta add?
twist.hint: Placeholder came first. What came next?

options.text: The first sign for an empty place.
options.feedback: The empty-place sign came before. Brahmagupta added rules for using zero as a number in sums.

options.text: Rules for using zero in sums.
options.feedback: Yes. Brahmagupta set out rules, like a number minus itself is zero, so zero could work as a number.

options.text: Proof that zero is just a gap, not a number.
options.feedback: It was the other way. His rules treated zero as a number with its own results.

transfer.stem: A shop's stock app in Nagpur shows 25 packets in and 25 sold, but leaves the 'left' box blank. Which of Brahmagupta's rules shows what it should read?
transfer.hint: Recall his rule for minus.

options.text: Blank is right, since zero is not a real number.
options.feedback: Brahmagupta treated zero as a number. 25 minus 25 gives zero, a real answer.

options.text: 25, since no new stock came in.
options.feedback: All 25 were sold. A number minus itself leaves zero, not the number you started with.

options.text: 0, since a number take away itself is 0.
options.feedback: Right. By Brahmagupta's rule, 25 minus 25 is zero, so the box should show 0.

twist.stem: How did the digits get from India to Fibonacci?
twist.hint: Follow the digits west.

options.text: A scholar wrote of them in Arabic.
options.feedback: Yes. A scholar wrote of India's digits in Arabic, and later Fibonacci took them to Europe.

options.text: Europe making its own 0 to 9.
options.feedback: Europe did not make its own. The digits came from India through Arabic writing.

options.text: Traders from Babylon took them west.
options.feedback: The Babylonians had place value but no zero. India's digits went west through Arabic books.

transfer.stem: At a tea stall in Lucknow, a man insists the digits on his rupee notes came from Arabia. What is the best reply?
transfer.hint: Where did the digits start?

options.text: They began in India, then went west.
options.feedback: Right. The digits came from India, a scholar wrote of them in Arabic, and that is why both names stick.

options.text: He is right; Arabia made them first.
options.feedback: Arabic writing carried the digits west, but they began in India. That is why they are called Hindu-Arabic.

options.text: Fibonacci made them up in Europe.
options.feedback: Fibonacci took the digits to Europe much later. They first came from India.

twist.stem: A museum display shows Bi Sheng's movable type as cast metal pieces. What should the fix be?
twist.hint: Recall the material he used.

options.text: His type was small pieces of baked clay.
options.feedback: Yes. Bi Sheng made the first movable type in China from baked clay, not metal.

options.text: No fix; early movable type was metal.
options.feedback: Bi Sheng's first movable type was baked clay. Metal type came later.

options.text: His type was carved as whole wooden pages.
options.feedback: Whole wooden blocks are block printing. Bi Sheng's movable type was small pieces of baked clay.

transfer.stem: A shop owner in Surat changes his price board each week. Which choice uses the movable-type idea?
transfer.hint: Which one reuses small pieces?

options.text: Paint a new board for each week's prices.
options.feedback: A new board each week is like carving a new block. Movable type reuses small pieces.

options.text: Number tiles he resets each week.
options.feedback: Right. Like movable type, a set of small pieces can be reset again and again for new prices.

options.text: One carved board kept for years.
options.feedback: A fixed board is like one woodblock for one page. Movable type lets the pieces be reset.

twist.stem: Jikji, from 1377, is the oldest surviving metal-type book. Does that mean metal type was first used in 1377?
twist.hint: Oldest surviving is not the same as first.

options.text: Yes; the oldest book marks the first use.
options.feedback: The oldest book still around is not always the first made. Koreans used metal type in the 1200s.

options.text: No; metal type began with Gutenberg.
options.feedback: Gutenberg came later. Metal type was used in Korea long before his Bible.

options.text: No; Koreans used metal type in the 1200s.
options.feedback: Yes. Metal type was in use in Korea in the 1200s. Jikji is just the oldest such book that survives.

transfer.stem: Neha's oldest family photo left is from 1965. Her grandmother recalls older photos that were lost. What can Neha fairly say?
transfer.hint: Oldest surviving is not the same as first.

options.text: No photos were taken before 1965.
options.feedback: The oldest one that survives is not always the first. Jikji is the oldest metal-type book left, yet metal type was used earlier.

options.text: Photos go back at least to 1965.
options.feedback: Right. Like Jikji, the oldest one left only shows a latest start date. Earlier ones may simply be lost.

options.text: The photo proves her grandmother is wrong.
options.feedback: A surviving photo cannot prove lost ones never existed, just as Jikji does not mark the first metal type.

twist.stem: In Gutenberg's shop, a printer's letter 'e' cracks while a page is set. What can he do with this kind of type?
twist.hint: His letters were cast alike.

options.text: Carve the whole page again.
options.feedback: That is block printing. Gutenberg's letters matched, so one piece could replace another.

options.text: Stop until a new block is cut.
options.feedback: There is no block to cut. Gutenberg's type was single matching letters, so any 'e' fits.

options.text: Swap in any other 'e'.
options.feedback: Yes. Gutenberg cast matching metal letters, so any piece of the same letter could swap in.

transfer.stem: A village gets free tablets loaded with books, but many older people there cannot read. What changes at once?
transfer.hint: Ask who can use a book today.

options.text: Most people soon read, since books teach reading.
options.feedback: Books help readers, but they do not teach reading. Those who cannot read need lessons first.

options.text: Readers gain; others need lessons.
options.feedback: Right. Print put knowledge within reach of readers. Those who cannot read still have to learn first.

options.text: Nobody can use the tablets.
options.feedback: Those who can read gain right away. Only the others need lessons first.

twist.stem: Two nobles serve Akbar, one at 1,000 zat and one at 3,000 zat. Who likely got more pay?
twist.hint: What did a higher zat bring?

options.text: The one at 1,000, since lower numbers ranked higher.
options.feedback: A higher zat meant a higher rank, not a lower one, and more pay with it.

options.text: Neither; zat set rank but not pay.
options.feedback: Zat set both a noble's rank and his pay, so the two went together.

options.text: The one at 3,000.
options.feedback: Yes. Zat set a noble's rank and his pay, so a higher zat meant more pay.

transfer.stem: A cricket academy in Mohali gives each coach a grade number that sets pay. Each coach must also bring a set number of trainees. Which part of a mansab matches the trainees?
transfer.hint: A mansab came with an army task.

options.text: The zat number, which sets rank and pay.
options.feedback: Zat set rank and pay, like the grade number. The duty to bring trainees matches the horsemen.

options.text: A jagir, the right to an area's revenue.
options.feedback: A jagir was how pay came, as rights to an area's revenue. The trainee duty matches the horsemen.

options.text: The duty to keep horsemen.
options.feedback: Right. A mansabdar had to keep a set number of horsemen, just as each coach must bring trainees.

twist.stem: A jagirdar's son plans to sell the jagir's fields to a merchant. What is wrong with his plan?
twist.hint: What did the grant actually give?

options.text: No problem; a jagir was family land.
options.feedback: A jagir was a right to an area's revenue, not land the family owned.

options.text: It was not his land to sell.
options.feedback: Yes. A jagir gave the right to collect an area's revenue. The land was not his to sell.

options.text: The merchant must pay tax first.
options.feedback: The issue is ownership. A jagir was a right to revenue, so the fields were not the family's to sell.

transfer.stem: A company pays its Delhi manager by letting him keep the rent from a shop in Pune, which an agent collects for him. Which Mughal idea is this most like?
transfer.hint: Who collected the money while the noble was away?

options.text: A jagir, income rights over a place.
options.feedback: Right. Like a jagir, he gets the income of a place far away, and others collect it for him.

options.text: A zat rank number.
options.feedback: Zat set rank and pay. Getting paid from a far place's income is what a jagir did.

options.text: A gift of the shop for him to own outright.
options.feedback: He keeps the rent, not the shop. A jagir too was a right to income, not land to own.

twist.stem: Two farmers in one zabt circle grow different crops, wheat and cotton. Do they pay the same tax rate?
twist.hint: Taxes were set for each what?

options.text: Yes; one rate covered the whole province.
options.feedback: Each province was split into circles, and each crop had its own rate.

options.text: No; each crop had its own rate.
options.feedback: Yes. Under zabt, each circle had set rates for each crop, so wheat and cotton paid different rates.

options.text: Yes; one rate covered each circle.
options.feedback: Circles had rates for each crop, not one rate for all, so the two farmers paid different rates.

transfer.stem: A city plans a house tax based on measured house sizes, but half the houses have never been measured. What does zabt's story suggest?
transfer.hint: What did Todar Mal's method rest on?

options.text: It works only where houses are measured.
options.feedback: Right. Zabt worked where officials could survey land and keep careful accounts, and failed where they could not.

options.text: It works the same everywhere if the rate is high.
options.feedback: A high rate does not fix missing records. Zabt needed surveys and careful accounts to work.

options.text: Records do not matter; one rule fits each area.
options.feedback: Zabt did not work in provinces without surveys and accounts, so records matter.

twist.stem: Did the 1600 charter give the East India Company rule over land in India?
twist.hint: What did the charter actually grant?

options.text: Yes; it made the Company a ruler from day one.
options.feedback: The charter gave trade rights only. Land and power came much later.

options.text: Yes, over the coast where it traded.
options.feedback: The charter gave no land. It gave the sole English right to trade with the East.

options.text: No; it gave trade rights only.
options.feedback: Yes. The charter shut out other English traders, but it gave trade rights, not rule.

transfer.stem: A college gives one canteen firm the sole right to sell food on campus. What can that firm now do, and what can it not do?
transfer.hint: A sole right to trade is not a right to rule.

options.text: Run the whole college, since it holds the sole right.
options.feedback: A sole right to sell is not a right to run things. The Company's charter too gave trade, not rule.

options.text: Sell without campus rivals, but not run the college.
options.feedback: Right. Like the Company's charter, it shuts out rivals in trade but gives no power to govern.

options.text: No change; rivals can still sell on campus.
options.feedback: A sole right shuts out rivals, as the charter shut out other English traders.

twist.stem: Which order of events is right?
twist.hint: Look at the years.

options.text: Plassey, Buxar, then the diwani.
options.feedback: Yes. Plassey came in 1757, Buxar in 1764, and the diwani in 1765.

options.text: The diwani, Plassey, then Buxar.
options.feedback: The diwani came last, in 1765, after the wins at Plassey in 1757 and Buxar in 1764.

options.text: Buxar, the diwani, then Plassey.
options.feedback: Plassey came first, in 1757. Buxar followed in 1764 and the diwani in 1765.

transfer.stem: A foreign firm used to send money from its head office to buy goods in India. Then it gains the right to collect local rents in a district. What happens to the money from the head office?
transfer.hint: What did Indian revenue start to pay for?

options.text: It is no longer needed for goods.
options.feedback: Right. As with the diwani, local revenue now pays for the goods, so money from abroad stops flowing in.

options.text: It doubles to match the new rent.
options.feedback: After the diwani, money from India paid the Company's costs, so outside money stopped. It did not grow.

options.text: It stays the same as before.
options.feedback: After the diwani, money from India paid for cloth, troops and buildings, so gold from Britain stopped.

twist.stem: A letter from 1850 is signed by the Company's Governor-General in India. Does that fit the timeline?
twist.hint: When did the powers move?

options.text: Yes; Company rule went on until 1858.
options.feedback: Yes. The Company kept its powers until the law of 1858 moved them to the Crown.

options.text: No; the Crown ruled from 1765.
options.feedback: 1765 was the diwani, given to the Company. The Crown took over only in 1858.

options.text: No; the Company lost its powers after Plassey.
options.feedback: Plassey added to the Company's power. It kept its powers until 1858.

transfer.stem: A new state law in Karnataka moves a private bus company's routes to the state transport body, and its manager gets a new title. Which change is this most like?
transfer.hint: A law moved control and gave a new title.

options.text: The 1765 diwani grant to the Company.
options.feedback: The diwani gave the Company a right to collect tax. Powers moving by law with a new title is 1858.

options.text: The 1600 charter for trade in the East.
options.feedback: The charter gave trade rights. Powers moving by law with a new title is the change of 1858.

options.text: The 1858 move of powers to the Crown.
options.feedback: Right. In 1858 a law moved the Company's powers to the Crown, and the Governor-General became the Viceroy.

twist.stem: Did the Assembly first meet before or after India became free?
twist.hint: Recall the month and year it first met.

options.text: After, in late 1947.
options.feedback: It first met in December 1946. India became free later, in August 1947.

options.text: Before, in 1946.
options.feedback: Yes. It first met in December 1946, some months before India became free.

options.text: In 1950, when the Constitution began.
options.feedback: 1950 is when the Constitution came into force. The Assembly first met in December 1946.

transfer.stem: A housing society in Pune forms a committee to write its rules. Each building's own committee picks the members. Which Assembly feature is this like?
transfer.hint: Most were not chosen at a voting booth.

options.text: Members chosen by a direct vote of the people.
options.feedback: Here residents do not vote directly. Most Assembly members were not picked by a direct vote either.

options.text: Picked by the assemblies of the provinces.
options.feedback: Right. Most Assembly members were picked by provincial assemblies, just as building committees pick these members.

options.text: Members chosen by the British king.
options.feedback: Most Assembly members were picked by provincial assemblies, and the rest came from princely states.

twist.stem: A classmate claims Dr B.R. Ambedkar wrote the whole Constitution alone. What is the best reply?
twist.hint: Who wrote the first text, and who edited it?

options.text: His team drafted it; the Assembly changed it.
options.feedback: Yes. A team led by Dr Ambedkar wrote the draft, and the whole Assembly debated and changed it.

options.text: True; the Assembly passed his draft without changes.
options.feedback: The Assembly debated the draft and changed it, deciding 2,473 of the changes put forward.

options.text: He had no part in writing it.
options.feedback: He led the team that wrote the draft. The whole Assembly then debated and changed it.

transfer.stem: At a Bhopal college, a small team drafts new hostel rules. Then all the student reps debate them and change many lines. Which part of the Constitution's making does this match?
transfer.hint: A first text is not the final one.

options.text: One author writing the final text alone.
options.feedback: Here a team drafts and a larger body changes it, as the Assembly did with the draft.

options.text: The draft passing just as it was written.
options.feedback: The reps changed many lines, as the Assembly debated the draft and decided thousands of changes.

options.text: A draft, then debate and changes.
options.feedback: Right. Dr Ambedkar's team wrote the draft, and the whole Assembly then debated and changed it.

twist.stem: On what date did the Assembly adopt the text of the Constitution?
twist.hint: Adoption came first, two months earlier.

options.text: 26 January 1950.
options.feedback: That is when it came into force. The Assembly adopted the text two months earlier, on 26 November 1949.

options.text: 15 August 1947, at independence.
options.feedback: That is the day of independence. The text was adopted on 26 November 1949.

options.text: 26 November 1949.
options.feedback: Yes. The Assembly adopted the text on 26 November 1949, and it came into force on 26 January 1950.

transfer.stem: Sita signs a rent deal on 1 March that starts on 1 May. Which fact about the Constitution is like this?
transfer.hint: Signed one day, starting on another.

options.text: It was adopted and came into force on one day.
options.feedback: The text was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.

options.text: It came into force first and was adopted later.
options.feedback: It was the other way: adopted in November 1949, then in force in January 1950.

options.text: It was adopted, then in force two months on.
options.feedback: Right. Like the rent deal, it was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.
